tldr: By co-designing a log-barrier-smoothed ADMM solver and first-order reinforcement learning (SHAC) that reuses rollout solutions, the authors eliminate the two major bottlenecks of differentiable MPC—nonsmooth sensitivities and heavy computational costs—training a robust controller that never spins out in real full-scale car racing in just 7 minutes.
hero_caption: Overview of the proposed framework. (Top-left) Differentiable MPC solver using log-barrier smoothing to smooth gradients at active-set boundaries. (Top-right) First-order reinforcement learning (SHAC) pipeline that reuses rollout MPC solutions to avoid redundant re-solves. (Bottom) Combined with domain randomization, it trains end-to-end an MPC policy that remains robust even on harsh real-world race tracks with puddles.
overview:
Model predictive control (MPC) is a powerful control method capable of explicitly handling mathematical system models and operational constraints. In recent years, optimizing MPC parameters (such as neural-network-parameterized costs) end-to-end via reinforcement learning (RL) as differentiable MPC has gained significant attention. However, this approach faces two major hurdles. First, optimization sensitivities (gradients) become discontinuous across active-set transitions where constraints activate or deactivate, causing learning to stall. Second, evaluating an MPC policy requires solving an expensive optimization problem, which leads to prohibitive computational times whenever standard RL algorithms (such as PPO or SAC) re-evaluate data across multiple iterations.

To tackle this, the authors propose a co-design of the solver and the reinforcement learning pipeline. On the solver side, they develop "SmoothedTurboMPC," which integrates sequential quadratic programming (SQP) with an alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM) smoothed by log barriers on the GPU. Through closed-form proximal updates, it runs extremely fast on GPUs while delivering smooth, exact implicit sensitivities. On the learning side, they adopt Short-Horizon Actor-Critic (SHAC), a first-order reinforcement learning (FORL) method leveraging differentiable simulators. By reusing the MPC solutions obtained during rollouts directly for backpropagation, it completely eliminates wasteful re-solves from repeated policy evaluations.

In experiments, the approach achieved up to 4.4x higher end-to-end training throughput compared to existing differentiable MPC solvers (such as mpc.pytorch and acados). On an aggressive autonomous racing task, it achieved higher returns than MPC PPO with a 46x speedup, completing training on 3.3 million transitions in only 7 minutes. Finally, a policy trained with log-barrier smoothing and domain randomization was deployed onto a full-scale race car (Lexus LC500) and evaluated on a closed track featuring puddles at corner entries and exits. While a nominal baseline MPC with fixed parameters spun out in all trials, the policy learned with the proposed method stably and quickly completed all runs without failure.
contributions: Developed "SmoothedTurboMPC," a differentiable nonlinear MPC solver that integrates log-barrier smoothing with ADMM for the first time, computing smooth gradients at high speed with GPU parallelism.

Designed an efficient training pipeline combining first-order reinforcement learning (SHAC) and differentiable MPC that reuses optimization solutions from rollouts, eliminating redundant MPC re-evaluations.
Achieved up to a 4.4x throughput speedup over existing differentiable MPC frameworks, and demonstrated 46x faster training than PPO while obtaining higher-quality policies on a vehicle racing task.

Deployed an MPC policy trained with domain randomization RL onto a full-scale race car (Lexus LC500), validating its robustness by stably traversing puddle-covered corners with severe friction drops across all trials.

sections.heading: Background: Why do constraint changes break gradients?
sections.summary: Differentiable MPC computes gradients by applying the implicit function theorem (IFT) to the KKT conditions of the optimization problem. However, at active-set transitions where constraints switch on or off, the complementarity conditions break down, causing gradients to jump discontinuously and halting learning. Log-barrier smoothing is key to bridging this gradient gap smoothly.
sections.details:
### II-A Differentiable Optimization via Implicit Differentiation
At each control step, MPC solves a nonlinear program (NLP) consisting of an objective function alongside equality and inequality constraints. To differentiate this optimization problem end-to-end with respect to learnable parameters $\theta$ (such as cost weights), the implicit function theorem (IFT) is applied to the Karush-Kuhn-Tucker (KKT) conditions. By treating the KKT conditions as a root-finding problem, parameter gradients can be backpropagated efficiently by solving the adjoint equations using the Jacobian inverse at the optimal solution, without explicitly unrolling the optimization computational graph.

### II-B Active-Set Transitions and Log-Barrier Smoothing
However, there is a major pitfall. Because of the complementarity condition ($\nu \circ y_g = 0$) between inequality constraint slack variables $\nu$ and Lagrange multipliers $y_g$, the KKT Jacobian becomes singular at boundaries where constraints activate or deactivate (where both approach zero). As a result, sensitivities become undefined or experience discontinuous jumps.

Log-barrier smoothing addresses this issue. By perturbing the complementarity condition to $\nu \circ y_g = \kappa \mathbf{1}$ ($\kappa > 0$), it prevents both variables from dropping to zero at the same time. In a double integrator toy problem, under original hard constraints ($\kappa = 0$), gradient descent got trapped in local optima due to sharp objective gradient jumps at active-set switches. In contrast, with sufficient log-barrier smoothing ($\kappa > 0$), the gradients became smooth, reliably converging to the global optimum.

sections.heading: SmoothedTurboMPC: How it computes smooth gradients blazing fast on the GPU
sections.summary: Building upon the GPU-parallel solver TurboMPC, the authors introduce "SmoothedTurboMPC," combining log-barrier smoothing with ADMM. By explicitly retaining the log-barrier term in the inner quadratic subproblem (SAQP) without quadratic approximation and deriving closed-form proximal operator updates, it computes smooth sensitivities while maintaining GPU parallelism.
sections.details:
### III-A Smoothed SQP Formulation
In conventional sequential quadratic programming (SQP), log-barrier terms are often quadratically approximated into standard quadratic programs (QPs). However, this destroys the smoothing of the complementarity conditions at each step. SmoothedTurboMPC locally linearizes constraints and forms a quadratic objective approximation while explicitly retaining the convex log-barrier term $-\kappa \sum \log \nu_i$ in the convex subproblem.

### III-B SAQP: Smoothed ADMM QP Solver
To solve this subproblem containing log-barrier terms, the authors developed "SAQP (Smoothed ADMM QP)" as the inner solver. While standard ADMM handles inequality constraints by projecting onto the non-negative orthant, SAQP applies a proximal operator to the log-barrier term. This proximal problem decouples into scalar quadratic equations for each component, which can be solved in completely closed form via the positive root formula. Consequently, the smoothed complementarity condition holds exactly across all ADMM iterations, enabling branchless, fast GPU execution. For two-sided constraints (upper and lower bounds), a safeguarded Newton iteration solves the system to machine precision in just 7 iterations.

### III-C Implicit Differentiation and GPU Parallelism
In the backward pass, the method exploits the property that at convergence of the SQP, the KKT system of the subproblem coincides with that of the original smoothed NLP. This yields exact, smooth implicit sensitivities. Moreover, taking advantage of the stage-wise sparsity of MPC, both forward and backward passes are optimized to execute thousands of environment batches fully in parallel on the GPU. A quadratic penalty relaxation on slack variables is also integrated to prevent solver failures caused by intermediate constraint violations.

sections.heading: Accelerating Training: Why first-order RL (SHAC) instead of PPO?
sections.summary: Unlike direct neural network policies, evaluating an MPC policy requires solving an optimization problem. Algorithms like PPO or SAC that repeatedly re-evaluate collected data lead to explosive computation times. Instead, this work adopts SHAC, directly reusing the MPC solutions from differentiable rollouts in backpropagation.
sections.details:
### IV-A Reinforcement Learning Formulation for MPC Policies
The framework adopts a hierarchical structure where a neural network receives environment state $s$ and outputs MPC cost weight parameters $\theta$, which are then used to solve the MPC optimal control problem. For action exploration, Gaussian noise is added to the first control input $u_0^\star$ computed by the MPC.

### IV-B The True Computational Bottleneck in Learning MPC Policies
For direct neural network policies, environment stepping is typically the bottleneck, making off-policy or on-policy algorithms with repeated data reuse (e.g., SAC, TD3, PPO) favorable. For MPC policies, the opposite is true. Evaluating an action requires an MPC forward solve, and computing gradients requires a backward solve. Running multiple PPO epochs or repeatedly sampling states from a replay buffer to re-solve MPC drastically increases solver calls, inflating wall-clock time by $10\times$ to $27\times$.

### IV-C Computationally Efficient First-Order RL with SHAC
Therefore, this study adopts the first-order reinforcement learning algorithm Short-Horizon Actor-Critic (SHAC). SHAC performs short-horizon differentiable rollouts (e.g., 32 steps) and updates the policy (actor) in a single pass by combining running reward gradients with the critic value gradient at the terminal state. The crucial advantage here is that the optimal solutions and intermediate variables from the rollout MPC solves can be reused directly for backpropagation. Because the policy is updated with first-order gradients without re-solving a single additional forward pass, the total computational burden is dramatically reduced.

sections.heading: Experimental Results: 4.4x throughput, 46x faster training, and full-scale car puddle survival!
sections.summary: After demonstrating superior parallel throughput over existing solvers on synthetic benchmarks, the method achieved a 46x training speedup over PPO (finishing in 7 minutes) on an autonomous racing simulator. Furthermore, deploying an MPC trained with domain randomization onto a real race car proved outstanding stability on slippery surfaces.
sections.details:
### V-A Solver Speed and Scalability
A benchmark on constrained linear systems was performed on an RTX 5090 GPU. Scaling up to a batch size of $B=1024$, SmoothedTurboMPC was 13.9x faster than the state-of-the-art CPU solver acados, and 7.1x faster than the GPU-based mpc.pytorch. In end-to-end training throughput comparisons using SHAC, it recorded a 3.5x speedup over acados and a 4.4x speedup over mpc.pytorch.

### V-B Reinforcement Learning Efficiency in Autonomous Racing
Methods were compared on a challenging autonomous racing task (oval track driving) involving nonlinear tire friction and actuator limits.
- **Training Speed**: The proposed method (MPC SHAC) completed training in just 7.0 minutes (3.3 million transitions). In contrast, MPC PPO with the same MPC solver required 13 million transitions and took 5.35 hours (roughly 46x longer). Training the MPC policy finished in the same order of time as direct neural networks (Direct SHAC/PPO).
- **Performance**: MPC SHAC achieved a final normalized return of around 0.98, significantly outperforming MPC PPO (0.79) and direct neural network policies (0.72). It also dramatically reduced tracking error compared to a manually tuned nominal MPC.
- **Importance of Smoothing**: When using a hard-constraint solver without log-barrier smoothing (TurboMPC), active sets switched erratically across environments in the batch, causing severe noise in the aggregated gradients and destabilizing training even when using SHAC.

### V-C Real-World Demonstration on a Full-Scale Race Car (Lexus LC500)
An MPC SHAC policy was trained in simulation using domain randomization, randomizing road friction coefficients and introducing localized puddles (friction coefficient 0.6). This policy was deployed on a real Lexus LC500 on a closed course with actual puddles placed at corner entries or exits.
The manually tuned nominal MPC could not handle the sudden friction loss (model mismatch) from the puddle, resulting in severe spin-outs (peak sideslip angles of $35^\circ$ to $169^\circ$) in all 4 trials. In contrast, the trained MPC SHAC successfully completed all 4 trials (traversing puddles 12 times in total) with peak sideslip angles kept to only $3.5^\circ$ to $4.2^\circ$. Analyzing the learned cost function revealed that tracking weights for yaw rate and sideslip angle increased by approximately 100x over the nominal manual tune. This autonomously balanced aggression and caution, keeping the car safe in low-slip regimes while driving about 2 m/s faster on average.

captions.F6: Trajectory and telemetry data on the full-scale race car (Lexus LC500). When hitting the puddle (blue area), the manually tuned nominal MPC (grey) spun out (red 'x') in every trial. In contrast, MPC SHAC trained with the proposed method (green) kept sideslip angles minimal, safely and quickly completing the corner across all runs.

sections.heading: Conclusion and Future Work: Expanding to contact-rich robotic tasks
sections.summary: By combining smoothed ADMM on the GPU with first-order reinforcement learning (SHAC), this work establishes a framework for learning differentiable MPC policies with extreme speed and reliability. Future directions include learning system dynamics alongside cost weights and expanding to manipulation and legged locomotion involving contacts.
sections.details:
This paper resolves the long-standing challenges of computational expense and gradient discontinuity in differentiable MPC by tightly coupling the log-barrier smoothed SQP-ADMM solver "SmoothedTurboMPC" with first-order reinforcement learning "SHAC," which reuses optimization solutions.

As future work, the authors point to learning physical dynamics parameters concurrently with MPC cost functions. This raises new questions regarding how to balance the MPC's planner performance against the physical plausibility of the learned model. Additionally, expanding the framework to systems with hybrid discontinuous contacts, such as robotic contact-rich manipulation and legged locomotion, is planned.

sections.heading: Appendix: Penalty relaxation and mathematical treatment of two-sided inequality constraints
sections.summary: This section details the quadratic penalty relaxation formulation to prevent infeasibilities during training, as well as the safeguarded Newton method used to solve two-sided inequality constraints—crucial for actuator limits and track boundaries—without branching and down to machine precision on the GPU.
sections.details:
### Appendix A Inequality Constraint Relaxation via Quadratic Penalty
As parameters $\theta$ update during training, inequality constraints might become too restrictive, risking MPC infeasibility. To prevent this, slack variables $\xi$ are introduced with an added penalty $\frac{\gamma_\xi}{2}\|\xi\|^2$ in the objective. Even with this relaxation, the SAQP proximal updates remain closed-form, and the sensitivity matrices in the adjoint equations stay uniformly bounded, substantially improving numerical stability throughout training.

### Appendix B Extension to Two-Sided Inequality Constraints and Newton's Method
Doubling constraint rows for two-sided bounds ($h_l \le g(x) \le h_u$), such as actuator limits and track widths, wastes GPU resources. SmoothedTurboMPC imposes two-sided barrier terms $-\kappa \log \nu_l - \kappa \log \nu_u$ on a single row. The corresponding proximal update requires finding the root of a cubic equation; using a safeguarded Newton iteration starting from the midpoint, it achieves machine precision in just 7 iterations without any thread divergence on the GPU.

takeaways: When learning differentiable MPC policies, policy re-evaluation is far more computationally expensive than environment stepping, making first-order RL (like SHAC) that reuses solutions vastly superior to iterative reuse algorithms like PPO.

Without proper log-barrier smoothing of inequality complementarity conditions, gradient noise explodes at active-set transition boundaries during batch training, causing policy optimization to stall or fail.

Replacing the standard ADMM projection step with a log-barrier proximal operator (via closed-form quadratic roots or a few Newton iterations) achieves both smooth sensitivities and high GPU parallel efficiency.
Applying domain randomization RL to a structured MPC framework yields real-world controllers that exhibit extreme robustness against unseen disturbances (like puddles) with very short training times.
limitations: Applying first-order reinforcement learning (SHAC) requires a differentiable environment simulator (or a learned dynamics model that provides surrogate gradients).
The current implementation is restricted to tuning MPC cost weight parameters and does not address the simultaneous identification or learning of unknown physical dynamics parameters.
It cannot be directly applied to robotic tasks with explicit contact discontinuities, such as foot impacts or object collisions (noted as future work).
